items.question: What is the difference between primary, secondary, and tertiary aging in this chapter?
items.notes: This is the core distinction the professor returned to throughout the session.

items.question: Why did the professor say the most practical interventions are aimed at secondary aging rather than primary aging?
pdf_evidence: ch05-gerontology secondary aging and lifestyle factors
items.notes: Likely follow-up if the student only lists the three aging categories without explaining why the distinction matters.

items.question: Why is the truck-driver sun-exposure photo a good example of secondary aging rather than primary aging?
pdf_evidence: ch05-gerontology skin change and sun exposure
items.notes: Tests whether the student can connect an example to the right category instead of just calling it aging.

items.question: Why should you explain this chapter in terms of function and autonomy, not only in terms of appearance?
pdf_evidence: ch05-gerontology cardiovascular, respiratory, and nervous system changes
items.notes: Likely when the student overfocuses on wrinkles, gray hair, or visible body changes.

items.question: How do sensory changes become a social interaction issue rather than just a body-part issue?
pdf_evidence: ch05-gerontology sensory change and social isolation
items.notes: The professor repeatedly linked hearing loss to misunderstanding behavior and communication.

items.question: What exactly changes in sleep in later life, and why do older adults say they did not sleep even when they did?
pdf_evidence: ch05-gerontology sleep quality in later life
items.notes: Likely when the student says only that older adults wake up early.

items.question: Why did the professor warn you not to treat one biological aging theory as the whole explanation of aging?
items.notes: Tests whether the student understands the plural, competing-theory structure of the chapter.

items.question: What is the design limitation of the 34, 60, 78 age-break article the professor showed?
items.notes: Likely when the student repeats the age-break claim without explaining that the evidence shown was cross-sectional.

items.question: How does terminal decline change the way you think about age versus distance to death?
items.notes: This checks whether the student can explain the professor's time-to-death framing rather than just naming tertiary aging.

items.question: How should you separate the assigned chapter from the supplementary anti-aging material on Hallmarks of Aging and David Sinclair?
items.notes: Likely when a student blends textbook content and current anti-aging discourse into one undifferentiated answer.

items.question: What social or ethical problem did the class discussion raise about extending life much further?
items.notes: Useful if the student wants to connect the chapter to broader aging-society questions without losing the reading anchor.
